<li>
<p>We read <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.9694em;vertical-align:-0.2861em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.1389em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.10764em">f</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.10764em">f</span><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2861em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> and multiply to get the output of the first feedforward layer</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>We read <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.9694em;vertical-align:-0.2861em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.1389em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.10764em">f</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.10764em">f</span><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2861em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> and multiply to get the output of the second feedforward layer</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>We read the output from step 5 and add it to the output of step 7, then perform layernorm</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>We read the unembedding layer, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.1514em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.1389em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">u</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.0883em;vertical-align:-0.247em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em"><span style="top:-2.453em;margin-left:-0.1389em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span></span></span><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em">T</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.247em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> then multiply to get the token logprobs for the prompt sequences</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Across steps 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 we read all parameters of the model. On step 3, we perform the attention op which, using FlashAttention, requires far less memory bandwidth than reading the model weights (for reasonable length sequences and batch sizes). On all steps, we read activations, which are matrices that are negligible compared to the model size (also for reasonable length sequences and/or batches). Note that this is the memory requirement <strong>for all tokens</strong>.</p>
<p>The bottomline, the memory requirement per token for prompt processing is significantly less than generating tokens, because we batch the matrix multiplication across the sequence dimension for prompts!</p>
<h4 id="memory-bandwidth-needed-for-model-weights" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#memory-bandwidth-needed-for-model-weights" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Memory bandwidth needed for model weights</h4>
<p>The model weights in 16-bit precision take up <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">70</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">140</span></span></span></span> GB of memory.</p>
<h4 id="memory-bandwidth-needed-for-kv-cache" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#memory-bandwidth-needed-for-kv-cache" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Memory bandwidth needed for KV cache</h4>
<p>The size of our KV cache is the size of all keys in values for all heads for all layers in the neural net, for all of the previous tokens, which is 320 MB per token and batch element.</p>
<p>Llama 2 decided to <a href="https://x.com/amanrsanger/status/1657095380650311681?s=20" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">remove multi-head attention</a>. But instead of multi-query attention, they use grouped query attention, which improves performance. This results in 8 heads (or groups) for the keys and values, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7167em;vertical-align:-0.2861em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">n</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.1514em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.03588em">g</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2861em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, rather than the normal 128 for multi-head, and 1 for multi-query.</p>
<p>For <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span> tokens, the size of our KV cache will be <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.9805em;vertical-align:-0.2861em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">n</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.1514em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8141em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8141em"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">5</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>. Using 16-bit precision, that makes it <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">320</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span> KB. Given a batch size <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span></span></span></span>, we get <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">320</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span></span></span></span> KB.</p>
<p>For completions, this gives the memory requirement per token of:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">Memory / token</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em"></span><span class="mord">140</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">GB</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">320</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> KB</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<p>The first term dominates for shorter sequences/small batches. Otherwise, the second term is much larger. However, since we only have 160 GB of memory and the model takes up 140 GB, the KV cache will impose a small cost on memory bandwidth in our experiments.</p>
<p>The memory bandwidth for prompts is around:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">Memory / token</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:2.0074em;vertical-align:-0.686em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mopen nulldelimiter"></span><span class="mfrac"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:1.3214em"><span style="top:-2.314em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:3em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span><span style="top:-3.23em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:3em"></span><span class="frac-line" style="border-bottom-width:0.04em"></span></span><span style="top:-3.677em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:3em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">140</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.686em"><span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose nulldelimiter"></span></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord"> GB</span></span></span></span></span></span>
<h3 id="communication-overhead" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#communication-overhead" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Communication overhead</h3>
<p>For simplicity, we ignore communication costs as accounting for model parallelism will significantly complicate things. We can reasonably assume that it won’t add a large enough slowdown for any of our calculations (especially since we are only splitting Llama across 2 GPUs).</p>
<h2 id="prompt-processing-is-really-cheap" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#prompt-processing-is-really-cheap" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Prompt processing is really cheap</h2>
<p>Prompt processing or the <em>time to first token</em> is the most efficient part of transformer inference, and you should expect 3x price cuts relative to GPT-3.5.</p>
<p>For a model with <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">P</span></span></span></span>-parameters and an <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span>-length prompt, the memory requirement for processing a prompt is about <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">P</span></span></span></span> Bytes, while the compute requirement is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.13889em">P</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span> FLOPs. Since A100s can handle 312 TFLOPs of matmul and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, we are compute-bound for sequence lengths <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7224em;vertical-align:-0.0391em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">&gt;</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">156</span></span></span></span>. 9</p>
<p>On A100s, FLOPs utilization will likely max out just a bit under 70% MFU. This amounts to around 200 TFLOPs. 2-80 GB A100s will cost us around $4.42/hr 10, which comes out to 0.0012/second. The FLOPs requirement for Llama is 140 TFLOPs/token. Given the aggregate FLOPs for 2 A100s, we can calculate what the tokens per second should look like:</p>

<p>That&#x27;s a price of:</p>
<p><strong>$0.00042 / 1K tokens</strong></p>
<p>Compared to GPT-3.5’s <strong>$.0015</strong> this is a steal! To be precise, it’s an almost 4x price decrease!</p>
<p>Latency is also quite good! On our 2 GPUs with a batch size of 1, We should be able to process 512 tokens in 170ms and 1536 tokens in 530ms.</p>
<p>Let’s validate these claims with actual numbers. We use an internal fork of huggingface’s text-generation-inference repo to measure cost and latency of Llama-2.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 2: Each datapoint measures a different batch size. For prompt tokens, we always do far better on pricing than gpt-3.5, but trail slightly behind on gpt-3.5&#x27;s latency of 0.4s for 3.6K tokens." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-1.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-1.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-1.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 2: Each datapoint measures a different batch size. For prompt tokens, we always do far better on pricing than GPT-3.5, but trail slightly behind on GPT-3.5&#x27;s latency of 0.4s for 3.6K tokens.</figcaption></figure>
<p>As we can see the price is <em>significantly</em> better than GPT-3.5’s $0.0015/1k tokens! It does look like we lag a bit behind on time to first token for longer sequences, but the solve is quite straightforward. Parallelizing Llama across 8 GPTs (instead of 2) would give us an almost 4x speedup, meaning Llama-2 dominates GPT-3.5 for prompts!</p>
<h2 id="generating-tokens-is-slow-and-very-expensive" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#generating-tokens-is-slow-and-very-expensive" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Generating tokens is slow and very expensive</h2>
<p>In theory, it is possible to get <strong>competitive pricing</strong> to GPT-3.5 on completions, but in practice, you’ll likely do worse.</p>
<p>When generating tokens, we move from compute-bound to memory-bound. 11. Assuming, a batch size of 1, let’s determine the throughput we can achieve.</p>
<p>Each 80 GB A100 has peak memory bandwidth of 2TB/s per GPU. However, like FLOPs utilization, you can probably expect closer to 60–70% of that in inference workloads (1.3 TB/s). Since the KV cache is negligible at small batches, our throughput on 2-A100s will be:</p>
<span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:2.4271em;vertical-align:-0.936em"></span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8141em"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" <p>Our new prices are much worse. At $0.0012/sec, we’re getting a cost of...</p>
<p><strong>$0.066 / 1K tokens</strong></p>
<p>This is abysmal pricing and speed for a GPT-3.5 level model! But remember the note from earlier on batch sizing. We’re so memory bottlenecked that we can increase the batch size with no drop in generation speed. The higher our batch size, the lower our costs.</p>
<p>We can’t increase to infinity, as our KV cache will eventually take up all of GPU RAM. Luckily, grouped-query attention helps alleviate this issue. For <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span></span></span></span> tokens, a batch size of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span></span></span></span>, and 16-bit precision, our cache will be <span class="katex"><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3.2</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.05017em">B</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span><span class="mbin">⋅</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8141em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8141em"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">5</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> Bytes. In the case of 4096 tokens, this equates to 1.3 GB of memory for a batch size of 1. We have 160 GB of space on our 2-A100 machine. Our model takes up 135 GB of this, leaving just 25 GB of space for the KV cache. Due to additional inefficiencies in memory storage. our max batch size for longer sequence lengths is around 8.</p>
<p>Given the (roughly) 8x speedup, we can expect a price of <strong>$0.00825 / 1K tokens</strong>. This is still worse than GPT-3.5-turbo, but closer. For shorter sequence lengths (1k total tokens), we should be able to increase the batch size to 32, meaning a price of <strong>$0.00206 / 1K tokens</strong>. In theory, this is competitive with GPT-3.5-turbo.</p>
<p>Another solution is increasing the number of GPUs. By renting 8-80 GB A100s, we get 1.28TB of memory. Removing the model weights, we have over 1TB of memory left over for the KV cache, meaning a batch size of &gt;512 tokens is possible. Note that we won’t actually see a 512x cost decrease, as the KV cache now takes up 8x more memory bandwidth than the model size, meaning it would be closer to a 64x cost decrease.</p>
<p>Using more compute also solves the latency issue. GPT-3.5 hits around 70 TPS. Splitting the model across 8GPUs instead of 2 should bring us around 74.4 tokens/s.</p>
<p>We didn’t have access to 8 A100s when running this experiment, but let’s take a look at the numbers on 2-80 GB A100s:</p>
<h2 id="measured-generation-performance" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#measured-generation-performance" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Measured generation performance</h2>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Figure 3: For all datapoints, we measure price per generated tokens when generating 512 tokens." loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-2.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-2.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fllama-inference-2.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div><figcaption>Figure 3: For all datapoints, we measure price per generated tokens when generating 512 tokens.</figcaption></figure>
<p>These numbers are pretty close to what one would expect given the memory bandwidth calculations.</p>
<p>As we can see, increasing the batch size directly results in almost linearly decreasing costs for price/1K tokens. However, we still trail a decent bit short of GPT-3.5 pricing of $0.002/1K tokens — especially for longer sequence lengths.</p>
<h2 id="large-batch-sizes-mean-unacceptable-latency" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#large-batch-sizes-mean-unacceptable-latency" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Large Batch Sizes Mean Unacceptable Latency</h2>
<p>Running generation with large batch sizes means GPT-3.5 competitive pricing, but it spikes the time to first token. As we increase our batch size, costs go down linearly, but time-to-first token also increases linearly.</p>
<p>A batch size of 64 brings us to better pricing than GPT-4. But, a batch size of 64 gives us:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>A time to first token of almost <strong>3 seconds</strong> for only 512 tokens!</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>A batch size of 64 for 3596 tokens is <strong>20.1 seconds</strong>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>As a result, the kinds of workloads where Llama-2 would make sense relative to OpenAI’s API are:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p>A large prompt with little to no generated tokens — handling pure prompts is remarkably simple.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Generating tokens with a small or no prompt — we can tune the batch size up to &gt;64 and get competitive pricing with GPT-3.5-turbo without sacrificing latency.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Offline batch-processing jobs that are not latency-critical.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Turning up the batch size requires consistently large workloads, which most startups will not have! For most users and most workloads, usage is incredibly bursty. Of course, a candidate solution is auto-scaling up and down on-demand GPUs, but even so, you can probably expect on average 50% of max throughput per-GPU — especially given cold boot times.</p>
<p>Our recommendation is to use open-source models for prompt-heavy tasks and leave generation-heavy tasks to closed-source models like GPT-3.5</p>
<h2 id="quantization" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#quantization" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Quantization</h2>
<p>Most quantization methods are lossy, meaning some performance degradation. We can likely achieve mostly competitive performance with 8-bit quantization, giving a 2x price decrease on all calculated numbers! <strong>Quantization and imperfect utilization cancel each other out, meaning accounting for both, we expect similar prices to what we</strong>’<strong>e measured!</strong></p>
<p>However, the goal of most open-source quantization methods is to allow easy deployment on few/small consumer GPUs rather than optimized throughput at scale.</p>
<p>There are several open-source libraries that optimize for even lower precision quantization while maintaining performance. However, these libraries optimize for serving these models on few/small non-datacenter GPUs rather than throughput at scale. Specifically, they optimize for the low-batch inference case (mainly a batch size of 1). Despite offering (at best) 3–4x speedups, that still corresponds to a price of $0.017/1K tokens.</p>
<h4 id="bits-and-bytes" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#bits-and-bytes" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Bits and Bytes</h4>
<p>Bits and Bytes offers (effectively) lossless quantization, meaning no difference in performance. However, it’s main benefit is reduced memory usage rather than speed. For example the speedup of the recent NF4 representation is only on matmul speed, rather than inference throughput. Empirically, people don&#x27;t seem to be measuring speedups on that front.</p>
<p>It is also unclear how well it scales to larger batches.</p>
<h4 id="llamacpp" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#llamacpp" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Llama.cpp</h4>
<p>I believe Llama.cpp is mainly optimized for Apple hardware. They also have Cuda support, and support fast 4-bit precision for inference, but my suspicion is naive quantization here would result in significantly degraded performance.</p>
<p>Also, this library is optimized for the low-batch regime.</p>
<h4 id="gpt-q" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#gpt-q" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>GPT-Q</h4>
<p>GPT-Q is another quantization library. I have not tested GPT-Q, but plan on doing so. Hopefully we can see a 2x price reduction here!</p>
<p>Once more, the implementation is optimized for the low-batch regime. In addition, the &gt;3x speedup reported in the paper is only for 3-bit quantization, which is too lossy our use-cases.</p>
<h2 id="how-exactly-are-closed-source-models-cheaper" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#how-exactly-are-closed-source-models-cheaper" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>How exactly are closed source models cheaper?</h2>
<p>There are several methods closed-source models use to be dramatically speed up inference</p>
<h3 id="quantization-1" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#quantization-1" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Quantization</h3>
<p>As mentioned earlier, there are several solid open-source quantization methods - but I suspect OpenAI’s quantization implementations are better optimized for larger batches.</p>
<h3 id="mixture-of-experts" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#mixture-of-experts" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Mixture of Experts</h3>
<p>it is widely speculated GPT-4 uses mixture of experts 15. If GPT-3.5-turbo also uses MOE, then for the same level of performance you can serve a MUCH smaller (and therefore faster) model</p>
<h3 id="speculative-sampling" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#speculative-sampling" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Speculative sampling</h3>
<p>Speculative sampling is another interesting trick that gets around the slow decoding time of language models by having a smaller model draft several tokens in a row. 16. Note that in the limit this will not offer significant increases in <strong>throughput</strong>, but can drastically reduce latency. For reference, this <a href="https://github.com/dust-tt/llama-ssp" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">repo</a> implements a simplified version of it.</p>
<h3 id="fancy-tricks-for-inference-at-scale" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#fancy-tricks-for-inference-at-scale" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Fancy tricks for inference at scale</h3>
<p>When running inference at scale, OpenAI can probably do fancy things like allocate several 8-GPU nodes for prefilling a batch of requests, then allocate a single 8-GPU node for generating tokens on that batch of requests. This would give them the best of both worlds, where they can use batch sizes &gt; 64, and still see a ridiculously low time to first token.</p>
<h2 id="closing-thoughts" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#closing-thoughts" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Closing thoughts</h2>
<p>We’ve used these findings to inform how/when we decide to use Open-source models at Cursor.</p>
<p>To recap, we find it most helpful to use open-source models for prompt-heavy tasks, such as <strong>classification</strong> or <strong>reranking</strong></p>
<h2 id="come-work-with-us-at-cursor" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#come-work-with-us-at-cursor" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Come work with us at Cursor!</h2>
<p>We’re building <a href="https://cursor.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Cursor</a>, an AI-first code editor. When fundamentally re-imagining the development environment, we get to tackle loads of very interesting problems. For example, finetuning and serving models for a fraction of the price of OpenAI’s API. Or designing <a href="https://www.cursor.com/blog/prompt-design" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">new abstractions</a> for creating complex chains and agents with OpenAI’s API.</p>
<p>We’re a small team of 9 based out of SF and backed by OpenAI. If interested, please reach out at <a href="mailto:hiring@cursor.com" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">hiring@cursor.com</a>.</p>
<p>Or, if you want to talk shop about language models, DM me on <a href="https://x.com/amanrsanger" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Twitter</a>.</p>
